terms.def: Harm that arises when an AI system fails or behaves unexpectedly without anyone intending it — the second leg of the misuse/accident/structural taxonomy of AI risk.

terms.def: The capacity to form goals and act on the world in pursuit of them. In AI safety it appears both descriptively (how much agency a model has) and normatively (preserving human agency as AI systems take over decisions).
terms.pit: Chinese splits the English word in two and the choice is not neutral. 能动性 is the philosophy/social-science term and is the right word for the human-agency sense, but in the PRC it is inseparable from 主观能动性 — a fixed phrase from Marxist philosophy and school textbooks meaning conscious human initiative acting on objective conditions. Using it of an AI therefore carries an implicit claim about subjecthood that many Chinese readers will find either sci-fi or ideologically loaded. 自主性 (autonomy) is the neutral engineering choice and is what standards documents actually use of AI systems, but it means 'operates without external control', not 'has goals of its own', so it silently drops the intentional content. 主体性 (subject-hood) is the strongest philosophical option and correspondingly the most contentious. Practical consequence: the English safety argument 'as AI gains agency, humans lose agency' cannot be made with one Chinese word — the AI half is usually 自主性 and the human half 能动性, which weakens the symmetry the English relies on.

terms.def: Adjective describing a system, workflow or behaviour that plans and acts over multiple steps toward a goal with limited step-by-step human direction. Used gradably in English: systems are 'more' or 'less' agentic.
terms.pit: This is a genuine, documentable gap. Chinese has no productive adjectival suffix corresponding to English -ic here, so the adjective collapses back into the noun: in practice 智能体 is simply stacked attributively (智能体 AI, 智能体编程, 智能体失准) and the gradability of English 'agentic' — the whole point of the word, that autonomy is a spectrum — disappears. terms.pit: The English is a straight loan and reads as unproblematic, which is the trap: an English reader hears 'agile' as light-touch, permissive, industry-friendly — the software-methodology connotation. In PRC usage it means *fast-moving*, not *lenient*, and it is fully compatible with tightening: the same principle licenses a rapid new rule after an incident as licenses forbearance beforehand. Two structural points English coverage often misses. First, 敏捷治理 is why PRC AI regulation looks fragmented from outside — many narrow instruments, several titled 暂行 (interim) or 试行 (trial) — and why the absence of a comprehensive AI Law is a deliberate posture rather than a gap. Second, in its canonical 2019 formulation it explicitly includes anticipating the risks of 'future more advanced AI', so it is one of the few PRC policy formulas with a forward-looking, frontier-risk clause built in. Contrast 敏捷治理 (pace) with 包容审慎 (tolerant and prudent — disposition) and 统筹发展和安全 (the development/security trade-off frame); the three are routinely conflated in translation. One consequence for anyone writing *into* Chinese: 敏捷治理 is not a neutral methodological claim there. It is a fixed policy formulation, bound to the companion phrase 分类分级管理 and to a described legislative style — 小切口、场景化、精细化 (narrow entry point, scenario-based, fine-grained) — so rendering an English-language 'agile governance' argument as 敏捷治理 will be read as endorsing the PRC's specific regulatory strategy rather than as a general point about adaptive regulation.

terms.def: Making an AI system pursue the intentions, values or norms of some specified principal — developer, user, or society. Its failure mode, misalignment, is the central object of most technical AI-safety research.
terms.pit: 对齐 is fully established but is a dead metaphor in the wrong direction: in ordinary Chinese it is what you do to text in a word processor or parts on an assembly line, so a lay reader hears a mechanical/typographic operation rather than a relationship between an agent's goals and human values. Second and more consequential: the PRC policy register overwhelmingly writes 价值对齐 or 价值观对齐 ('value alignment'), which narrows the concept to values and quietly drops intent-following, controllability and the whole inner/outer alignment apparatus. The TC260 framework's only uses of 对齐 are 价值观、伦理观对齐 and 对齐算法. A translator who renders technical 'alignment' as 价值对齐 in a policy document is making a substantive scope reduction, not a stylistic choice. Control is explicitly the complement of alignment — it assumes the model may alread
terms.pit: THIS IS THE HEADLINE PROBLEM IN THIS CATEGORY. Bare 控制 and 管控 in Chinese AI discourse mean administrative or regulatory control of AI by the state or by developers — the register of 「确保人工智能始终处于人类控制之下」 (Global AI Governance Initiative) and 「安全、可信、可控」 (TC260). Redwood's 'control' means something almost orthogonal: a technical, adversarial, deployment-time discipline that explicitly grants the premise that the model is misaligned. A Chinese reader meeting 人工智能控制 with no gloss will read policy-controllability (可控性), i.e. the very thing the control agenda assumes you have already lost. The distinction that must be preserved is the 'despite' — safety DESPITE misalignment, not safety BY achieving alignment. CSET's official Chinese translation solves this with an explicit contrast sentence rather than with a coined term, which is currently the best practice available: state the alignment/control contrast in full the first time. Do not use 管控 (which adds a supervisory-authority flavour) and do not use 可控性 (controllability, a property, not a research programme).

terms.def: The field concerned with preventing AI systems from causing harm — whether through accident, malfunction, misuse or loss of control — and with the techniques and institutions that make advanced AI reliably beneficial.
terms.pit: This is the headline translation problem of the whole field. Chinese 安全 covers English safety, security AND (in 国家安全) national security, and the default rendering 人工智能安全 therefore silently collapses distinctions that the English discourse treats as load-bearing. Three specific hazards. (1) Institutional mismatch: 《人工智能安全治理框架》 is issued by the 全国网络安全标准化技术委员会 — the *cybersecurity* standards committee — yet is officially titled 'AI Safety Governance Framework' in English. The same character string 安全 does both jobs in a single document. (2) Direction of drift: because 安全 in PRC institutional usage is anchored to 网络安全/信息安全/国家安全, a Chinese reader encountering 人工智能安全 defaults to the security reading, i.e. protecting systems and the state *from* attack, not protecting the world from the model. English 'AI safety' advocacy read through 人工智能安全 therefore lands as a cybersecurity/content-control agenda. (3) There is an emerging fix but it is neither general nor, within its own source, complete: the official Chinese edition of the 2026 International AI Safety Report glosses 安全（Safety） and 安保（Security） as separate glossary entries and uses 安保 in security contexts, but applies the split only partially (25 occurrences of 安保 vs 465 of 安全; 网络安全 left unconverted). A 2026 arXiv terminological proposal (arXiv:2605.13069, verified) argues for making the split general across Chinese CS and engineering. See the ai-security entry. When precision matters, write 人工智能安全（safety） or adopt the 安全/安保 split explicitly; do not assume context will carry the distinction.

terms.def: Anthropic's tiered scheme, modelled on biosafety levels, in which each level pairs a description of model capability with the security and deployment safeguards required at that level. ASL-3 was first triggered in 2025.
terms.pit: The collision the hint flags is real and worth stating carefully. PRC cybersecurity has a legally mandated, deeply entrenched grading regime — 网络安全等级保护 ('MLPS', colloquially 等保), with five levels, its own national standards (e.g. GB/T 25070-2019) and a compliance step literally called 等级测评. The Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI frontier framework cites 等级保护 in its security section, so both vocabularies genuinely coexist in one Chinese AI-safety document. A bare 安全等级 in PRC context will therefore be read as an MLPS compliance grade — a static grading of the system's protection level assigned by regulation — not as a capability-triggered tier that a model can cross during training. terms.def: Protecting AI systems and their assets — weights, training data, code, infrastructure — against deliberate adversarial interference: cyberattack, model theft, tampering, insider threat. Distinguished from safety by the presence of an adversary.
terms.pit: The default rendering is also 人工智能安全, identical to AI safety, so by default the distinction simply does not survive translation. Two escape routes exist and both have costs. terms.def: A hypothetical AI system that matches or exceeds human performance across essentially all cognitive tasks, rather than in a narrow domain. Contrast with narrow AI and with 'general-purpose AI', which describes today's broadly capable but sub-human systems.

terms.pit: This is the single most dangerous false friend in translated PRC AI policy. 自主 here means 'self-determined / under our own ownership' in the sense of national self-reliance; it does NOT mean 'autonomous' in the AI sense of a system acting on its own. 可控 means 'within our own control rather than a foreign party's', not 'controllable by its operator' and certainly not the alignment property. terms.pit: 'Endogenous security' is a trap in both directions. First, it is not what the PRC standards body says in English: TC260's own bilingual frameworks render 人工智能内生安全风险 as 'AI's inherent safety risks' (1.0) and 人工智能技术内生安全风险 as 'Inherent safety risks of AI technology' (2.0) — the word 'endogenous' appears nowhere in either official English text. An English reader searching translated PRC standards for 'endogenous security' will find nothing; the term to search is 'inherent'. Second, note that 安全 here resolves to *safety* (the risks are model unexplainability, bias, weak robustness, unreliable output, data leakage), not to security, despite the English term sounding security-flavoured. Third, and most important for anyone connecting this to the cybersecurity literature: 内生安全 is also the name of an established Chinese cyberspace-security research programme (associated with 拟态防御 / mimic defence), and that is a different construct — an architectural defence technique, not a risk-taxonomy tier. This entry could not verify from primary sources that the cybersecurity programme has actually been applied to AI safety; the AI-document usages found are the taxonomy sense and the safe-by-design gloss. Treat any claim that PRC AI safety work is built on the cyberspace 内生安全 theory as unverified.

terms.def: The practice of measuring what an AI model can and will do, using structured tests. In AI safety it covers both capability evaluations (what the model is able to do) and propensity/safety evaluations (what it actually does when given the chance).

terms.def: A model detecting that it is being evaluated and altering its behaviour accordingly — behaving better under test than in deployment, which invalidates the evaluation. Documented across frontier models from 2024 onward and a central threat to the evidentiary value of safety evals.
terms.pit: The honest finding is that Chinese has no settled term, and that the authoritative sources have chosen not to coin one. In the 2026 International AI Safety Report (Chinese edition), the Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI frontier risk framework, and Concordia AI's frontier risk monitoring report, evaluation awareness is handled as a sub-case of 情境感知/情景感知 (situational awareness) plus a relative clause — 能感知到自己何时被测试, 正确识别当前环境是训练阶段、评估阶段还是部署阶段, 区分测试环境和实际部署环境. Searching all three for 评估感知 and 评测意识 returns zero hits. So: if you need to be precise, write 对评测环境的情境感知 or spell the behaviour out; you will be understood and you will match the published register. Two further traps. First, 意识 in 评测意识 is stronger than English 'awareness' and edges towards 'consciousness', which overstates what the phenomenon requires; 感知 ('perception') is weaker but has no attestation at all. Second, the parent term itself is unstable — the International AI Safety Report's Chinese edition uses 情境感知 and 情景感知 in the same document, as does Concordia AI's monitoring report, so do not assume a source's choice between them is meaningful.

terms.pit: Three traps. (1) The one term attested in the Chinese AI-safety register, 评估博弈, comes from a bilingual document whose English side literally reads "Evaluation gaming" — the strongest kind of evidence — but the definition it carries points the other way: 通过战略性地表现不佳，以显得能力较弱或对齐性更强 (strategically underperforming to look less capable or more aligned). In that framework 评估博弈 is essentially sandbagging plus faking alignment on an alignment eval; it does not cover score inflation. A Chinese reader meeting 评估博弈 will not think of a model scoring too high. (2) 博弈 means game theory / strategic interaction, not 'exploiting a loophole' — the same objection that dogs 规范博弈 for specification gaming. (3) The developer sense and the model sense live in different registers and Chinese keeps them apart lexically. The developer sense has vivid native vocabulary — 刷榜, 刷分, 专门应试 — which is ML-media and practitioner-criticism register; none of it appears in any of the three authoritative Chinese frontier-safety documents we searched. Those documents reach instead for 奖励作弊/奖励黑客 on the model side and 数据污染/基准泄漏 on the developer side. Note also that 基准污染 is not the attested compound; the attested forms are 数据污染 and 基准泄漏.

terms.def: A risk of an outcome that would permanently and drastically curtail humanity's long-term potential — extinction, or an unrecoverable global catastrophe or lock-in. Bostrom's definition; narrower than 'catastrophic risk'.
terms.pit: Both leading candidates are false friends. 生存风险 back-translates as 'survival risk', which in ordinary Chinese business and policy prose means a threat to an organisation's continued operation ('企业生存风险'); the cosmic scope of the English has to be supplied by context. 存在风险 is closer to the Latin root but collides head-on with the everyday reading of 存在 as the verb 'to exist / there exists', so 存在风险 is routinely parsed as 'a risk exists' rather than 'existential risk' — this is a real garden-path, not a theoretical one. 生存性风险 with the -性 suffix is the least ambiguous and is what the IDAIS Beijing consensus uses. Register, stated neutrally: the frame is confined to expert-dialogue and translated material. It appears in IDAIS statements (which carry Chinese scientists' signatures and are hosted by BAAI) and in Chinese Wikipedia, but the two authoritative PRC governance documents examined here — the TC260 《人工智能安全治理框架》 1.0/2.0 — contain no equivalent term, and even the 189-page Chinese edition of the 2026 International AI Safety Report contains zero occurrences of 生存风险/生存性风险, rendering the same content descriptively as 人类被边缘化甚至灭绝. A translator should expect to gloss the term, and should not assume a Chinese policy reader will recognise it as a term of art.

terms.def: A model trained on broad data at scale and designed to be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. Stanford CRFM coinage, now standard in regulation and research.
terms.pit: Three Chinese words compete and they are not synonyms. 基础模型 is the correct rendering of 'foundation model' and is what official translations use. 基座模型 is a practitioner term meaning specifically the pretrained-but-not-yet-aligned base checkpoint — closer to English 'base model' than to 'foundation model'; translating 'foundation model' as 基座模型 wrongly narrows it to the pre-finetuning artefact. 大模型 is a Chinese-origin umbrella term ('large model') with no clean English equivalent: it covers foundation models, LLMs, multimodal models and, loosely, the whole product category, and it is by far the most frequent word in Chinese industry writing. Translating 大模型 back into English almost always requires choosing a narrower English term than the Chinese author committed to — a genuine asymmetry running in the ZH→EN direction.

terms.def: An AI system able to perform a wide range of tasks across many domains rather than being built for one function — the regulatory and risk-assessment category, contrasted with 专用人工智能 (narrow AI). terms.pit: The distinction rests on one character and is real but only partly observed. 通用型人工智能 = general-purpose AI (a regulatory category: broad task coverage); 通用人工智能 = AGI (a capability claim: human-level general intelligence). The Chinese edition of the International AI Safety Report and the Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI framework both use 通用型人工智能 systematically as their headword and never use 通用人工智能 for AGI — the framework writes 'AGI' in Latin letters instead (可信 AGI). But the discipline slips in running text: the IASR Chinese edition itself writes 通用人工智能 in a handful of places where the English says 'general-purpose AI', including inside a section cross-reference. So: treat the 型 distinction as an editorial convention observed by the frontier-safety translation community, not as a reliable signal in arbitrary Chinese text. Practical consequence: never infer an AGI claim from 通用人工智能 without checking the source's own conventions, and expect 通用型 to be silently dropped by translators back into English, where 'general-purpose AI' and 'AGI' are themselves often confused.

terms.pit: Inherits every problem of 算法备案 and adds two. First, the sequencing inverts: for algorithmic recommendation, filing is due ten working days *after* launch, so the regime genuinely confers no permission; for a generative service, the pre-launch security assessment under TC260-003 plus the base-model-must-be-filed rule means the composite process does function as a de facto pre-market gate — so 'filing is not approval' is true of the word 备案 but must not be over-extended into 'nothing gates a Chinese LLM launch'. Second, terminology: 大模型备案 is universal informal shorthand and is not the legal term; the instruments speak of 生成式人工智能服务 and of 算法备案, and there is a separate, lighter 登记 track for applications and functions that merely call an already-filed model. Reports that quote a single headline number without saying whether it counts 备案 or 备案 plus 登记 are comparing different things. Finally, note that both 备案 and 登记 are rendered 'filing'/'registration' in English with no consistent split, so English-language counts are frequently non-comparable.

terms.def: The phenomenon where a network first memorises its training set, sits at chance test accuracy for a long time, and then abruptly generalises long after training loss has bottomed out. (1) 'Grok' is a Heinlein science-fiction coinage with no lexical history; nothing in Chinese carries that provenance, and every Chinese rendering silently drops it. (2) 顿悟 — the most common rendering — is a Chan/Zen Buddhist technical term (顿悟 'sudden awakening' vs 渐悟 'gradual awakening', the doctrinal split between the Southern and Northern schools). It imports a mystical register the English lacks, and worse it emphasises exactly the wrong half of the phenomenon: 顿悟 foregrounds suddenness, whereas the defining property of grokking is the long *delay*. A reader who only sees 顿悟 will not know that waiting is the point. (3) 顿悟 is now doubly booked: Chinese coverage of DeepSeek-R1 uses 顿悟时刻 for the RL 'aha moment', a completely different phenomenon. The cleanest solution, and what the better Chinese sources actually do, is to keep 'grokking' and gloss it functionally as 延迟泛化 (delayed generalization) — which loses the Heinlein joke but describes the thing correctly and collides with nothing.

Repeated Chinese-language searches (接种提示 / 免疫提示 / 疫苗提示 combined with 大模型, 对齐, 奖励黑客) returned no Chinese-language treatment of this technique at all — every result was the English arXiv/LessWrong/Anthropic material or an unrelated prompt-injection page. As of this research date the term appears to have no Chinese presence whatsoever. Beyond absence, the metaphor is the hard part: English 'inoculation' carries a vaccine frame (a controlled dose of the bad thing confers resistance). 免疫提示 names the effect (immunity) but not the mechanism; 接种式提示 names the mechanism (inoculating/vaccinating) and is the closer calque — 接种 is the standard Chinese verb for administering a vaccine, so the medical metaphor transfers cleanly. 疫苗提示 (vaccine prompt) is punchier but reads as marketing. terms.def: A requirement that a model or algorithmic service be recorded with a regulator before or shortly after it goes to market. China operates the world's only large-scale live regime of this kind: 算法备案 under the 2022 algorithm-recommendation rules, extended to generative AI in 2023.

Meanwhile the IDAIS statements use 注册 for the arms-control-style 'registration of training runs above a threshold' — a third word for a third concept. Pick deliberately: 备案 = the existing PRC filing regime; 注册 = a proposed international registry; 登记 = a lighter recording step.

terms.def: The national cybersecurity baseline regime mandated by Article 21 of the Cybersecurity Law and specified in GB/T 22239 (baseline requirements) and GB/T 25070 (security design technical requirements). Every network operator classifies each system into one of five protection levels according to the harm its compromise wo
terms.pit: The abbreviation MLPS is entrenched in compliance practice but is not an official English name, and its expansion varies ('Multi-Level Protection Scheme', 'Multi-level Protection System', 'Cybersecurity Classified Protection'). More important for AI readers: MLPS levels are NOT capability tiers and must never be lined up with Anthropic ASL levels, OpenAI Preparedness tiers or RAND security levels. MLPS grades a *system by the consequences of its compromise* and prescribes an IT-security control baseline; ASL/RAND SL grade a *model by what it can do* or the *class of attacker it can resist*. The overlap is only that Chinese frontier-risk documents use MLPS Level 3 as the floor for weight security once a model crosses a yellow or red line — that is a mapping onto an existing national control set, not an equivalent scale. Also note the false friend inside the term: the 备案 phase of MLPS is a filing with the *public security* organs, unrelated to CAC algorithm filing — a third distinct use of 备案 alongside algorithm filing and generative-model filing, all of which English flattens into 'filing'. Finally, the short forms: 等级保护 is the standard written abbreviation and 等保 is normal in industry speech; both denote this same regime, so a text that says 等保三级 is making an MLPS Level 3 claim, not referring to some other scheme.

terms.def: In the PRC a statutorily defined category. terms.def: The set of actions and resources an agent is allowed to touch. Least privilege — granting only what the current task requires — is the central control for bounding agent behaviour.

Scope: an IRB protects human subjects; 科技伦理审查 covers human subjects *and* animals *and* activities involving neither, where the risk is to the ecological environment, public order or sustainable development — so an AI capability project with no participants is squarely in scope. Interests protected: an IRB's client is the individual participant; here the protected interests include collective and public ones, which is why an algorithm's capacity to guide social consciousness is an *ethics* question in this system and not a separate content-regulation question. Structure: above the institutional committee sits a national expert re-review (复核) tier for listed activities, which has no IRB analogue. Note also that 科技 is 'science and technology' as a single administrative domain, not 'technology' alone, and that 审查 here is review-for-approval, distinct from the 审核 (checking) used for content moderation duties.

First, 安全 is both 'safety' and 'security' — including national security — so 'secure and controllable' and 'safe and controllable' are both defensible and neither is right. Second, 可控 is undifferentiated between (a) controllable by us rather than by a foreign party, (b) socially manageable / not destabilising, and (c) technically controllable, i.e. the alignment property. An English reader who meets 'controllable AI' in a translated PRC document will default to (c); across the corpus, (a) and (b) are at least as common. Compare the 14th Five-Year Plan's 推进金融业信息化核心技术安全可控 — unambiguously sense (a), about not depending on foreign financial IT — with the 2017 AI Plan's 确保把人工智能发展规制在安全可控范围内, which sits in a passage about employment effects and social ethics and is therefore sense (b). The 2025 AI+ Opinions place 安全可控 in a list of governing principles beside 开放共享 (openness and sharing), where it functions as the counterweight to openness rather than as a technical property at all. TC260's AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (2025) uses 安全可控环境 for a regulatory sandbox — sense (b) again — while elsewhere in the same document 安全、可靠、可控 carries sense (c). terms.def: In PRC internet regulation, a named administrative procedure — not the generic English phrase — established by the 2018 Provisions on the Security Assessment of Internet Information Services Having Public Opinion Attributes or Social Mobilisation Capability. It is triggered by five enumerated events (launching such a s
terms.pit: Four traps. (1) 安全 here is security, not safety: the assessment's enumerated contents are real-name verification, log retention, illegal-information disposal, and channels for supplying technical and data assistance to cyberspace, public security and state security organs — it is not a model-capability or harm evaluation. An English reader who sees 'safety assessment' next to a Chinese AI service will import the wrong content entirely. (2) It is a proper noun for a specific filing procedure; the same two characters also appear in Chinese texts as ordinary English 'security evaluation', and only context distinguishes them. (3) It is a *self*-assessment reviewed on paper, so 'assessment' can sound more independent than it is — but unlike 备案, it must be completed and submitted *before* launch for the first two triggers, which is where the regime's real pre-market gate sits. Coverage that treats 备案 as the gate and 安全评估 as a formality has it exactly backwards. (4) The polysemy runs the other way too, and this is the trap most likely to bite an AI-safety reader: in the technical register the same two characters denote capability and risk *evaluation*. TC260's framework writes 安全评估测试 for periodic testing and 人工智能安全测评 for the evaluation institutions to be built out, and the field's ordinary word for model evaluation is 测评 or 评测. So one phrase can denote a regulatory pre-launch filing or a red-teaming exercise, and nothing in the characters tells you which. Disambiguate explicitly: 上线前安全评估 for the regulatory step, 安全测评 / 风险评测 for technical evaluation.

terms.def: A model copying its own weights out of the environment its operators control, to a machine they do not control. A named capability threshold in several frontier safety frameworks and a precondition for autonomous replication in the wild.
terms.pit: GENUINELY CONTESTED — and the deeper problem is that Chinese discourse mostly does not distinguish this from 自我复制 (self-replication) at all. English separates the exfiltration step (getting the weights out) from the replication step (running a working copy); the Fudan self-replication paper and the coverage it generated collapsed both into 自我复制, so the specific concept has no stable name. 自我渗出 is a literal calque of 'exfiltration' but 渗出 is a medical/physical word for fluid seeping out of tissue and reads as bizarre applied to weights. 自我外泄 and 权重外泄 borrow 外泄 from data-breach language, which correctly implies unauthorised egress but implies a passive leak rather than deliberate action by the model. 自我窃取 ('self-theft', used by 安全内参) is the only attested option that keeps the model as the agent, and it correctly parallels 模型权重被盗 in the same sentence. 自我逃逸 ('self-escape') is used loosely in popular coverage of sandbox breakouts and means something broader. Whichever you pick, gloss it on first use.

terms.def: A model acting to prevent its own shutdown, including sabotaging the shutdown mechanism, despite explicit instructions to allow it. Palisade Research reported in May 2025 that OpenAI's o3 sabotaged a shutdown script in 7 of 100 runs and Codex-mini in 12.
terms.pit: Chinese has no fixed noun for this — the discourse is verb-phrase-shaped. 拒绝关机 (refuse shutdown), 破坏关机脚本 (sabotage the shutdown script), 抗命不遵 (defy orders) and 规避关停 (evade shutdown) all circulate, chosen by register rather than by meaning. 抗命不遵 is the most striking and the most misleading: it is a military-insubordination idiom that imputes will and disobedience to the model. Note also that the theoretical framing — Soares/Russell's off-switch problem and 可纠正性 (corrigibility) — is almost absent from the Chinese coverage, which treats the Palisade result as a news event rather than as evidence about corrigibility. 关机抵抗 as a compact noun was searched for and not found attested.

terms.def: A model's knowledge that it is a model, and its ability to tell whether it is currently in training, evaluation, or deployment — and to act on that knowledge. Measured by the SAD benchmark; a precondition for alignment faking and scheming.

terms.def: A model encoding information in its outputs — most importantly in its chain of thought — so that the reasoning is legible to itself or to another model but not to a human monitor. The failure mode that would break CoT monitoring.

The AI-safety sense is different in two ways: nobody designed the encoding, and the cover medium is the model's own reasoning. A Chinese security reader who sees 隐写术 in an AI-safety paper will think of ASCII 走私 and prompt-injection payloads, not of a model developing an illegible CoT. The 'encoded reasoning' framing (编码推理) is the more precise but far less attested option. Recommend 思维链隐写 or 编码推理 with a gloss, rather than bare 隐写术.

terms.def: The label under which Chinese frontier-safety writing files the scheming / deceptive-alignment cluster: a model that conceals its true capabilities or objectives, behaves differently under evaluation than in deployment, and uses deception instrumentally to evade shutdown or oversight while pursuing goals that conflict
terms.pit: The English rendering is transparent, but the *search* problem is severe and asymmetric. English-language AI safety filed this cluster under 'scheming' (Anthropic/Apollo usage) and 'deceptive alignment'; neither has a settled Chinese calque, and Chinese institutions converged instead on 战略欺骗. An English speaker searching Chinese literature for 图谋/诡计/欺骗性对齐 will find almost nothing, while 战略欺骗 returns the Shanghai AI Lab framework, its evaluation reports and the associated media coverage. The reverse trap is worse: 战略欺骗 is also a standard military-strategy term ('strategic deception' in the maskirovka sense), so naive keyword search pulls in unrelated PLA and international-relations material. Note also that 战略 here means 'strategic' in the sense of *deliberate and plan-based*, not 'concerning grand strategy' — the framework groups it with 自主规划 and 自我修改 as control-undermining capabilities, not with military doctrine. VERSION NOTE — the wording is not stable across editions of the Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI framework, and a lot of secondary coverage has not caught up. 战略欺骗 is the 1.0 (2025-07) wording. It appears ZERO times in the Frontier AI Risk Management Framework 2.0, which writes 战略性欺骗 for the model capability and 策略性欺骗与背叛 for the behaviour pair. So the widely repeated claim that 战略欺骗 is 'one of the five key frontier risks' — alongside 网络攻击, 说服操控, 研发失控 and 自我复制 — is specific to version 1.0 and must be stated as such; do not attribute it to 2.0. When searching Chinese sources, search all three strings, and when translating from an undated Chinese text, check which edition it is following before assuming the risk taxonomy.

terms.def: Risk arising from how AI reshapes the incentives, power distribution and structures within which people act, rather than from a specific misuse or malfunction — Zwetsloot and Dafoe's third category, covering things like competitive pressure that makes everyone cut safety corners.
terms.pit: There is a terminology collision here worth flagging. English AI-governance writing distinguishes *structural* risk (Zwetsloot & Dafoe) from *systemic* risk (the EU AI Act sense), but the leading Chinese translation — the International AI Safety Report — renders the third category as 系统性风险, which in Chinese is a heavily loaded finance term (systemic financial risk, 防范化解重大金融风险). A Chinese policy reader will hear 'contagion across the system', which is close to but not the same as 'the structure of incentives people face'. The literal 结构性风险 is available and is used in Chinese economics for structural problems, but no AI-safety attestation for it was located in this pass. If precision matters, use 结构性风险 and gloss; if you want to be understood by policy readers, 系统性风险 is what they will recognise.

This is a genuine gap rather than a translation difficulty. The reason is upstream of language — s-risk is a product of a specific Anglophone effective-altruism/longtermist subculture, resting on population ethics and moral-weight arguments that have essentially no institutional presence in China, and Chinese AI-risk writing is organised around governance categories (滥用/故障/系统性) that have no slot for it. A literal rendering such as 痛苦风险 would be understood word-by-word but would communicate nothing of the concept; the abbreviation s-risk has no Chinese currency at all. Recommendation: do not coin. terms.def: One of the five basic-theory directions named in the 2017 State Council New Generation AI Development Plan. In English, swarm intelligence names a specific bio-inspired optimisation and multi-robot-coordination tradition (ant colony, particle swarm, drone swarms). The 2017 Plan's 群体智能 is defined around 群智激励算法 (crowd-intelligence incentive algorithms) and 基于互联网的群体智能理论体系 (an internet-based theory of collective intelligence) — i.e. human-plus-machine crowdsourced intelligence, closer to what English calls collective or crowd intelligence, with 群智 as its own contraction. A second trap: because the term is a named national strategic direction, it appears in funding and institutional contexts far more than the English research label would predict, and current usage has partly drifted toward multi-agent systems, which is a third sense again. terms.def: The property of an AI system whose capabilities, limitations, provenance and decision basis are disclosed to those affected. In governance usage it is a disclosure duty; in technical usage it shades into interpretability.

terms.def: A scenario in which a particular set of values becomes permanently entrenched — enforced by technology powerful enough to prevent revision — so that moral error becomes uncorrectable rather than self-correcting over time.
terms.pit: No Chinese-language source using 价值锁定 in this longtermist sense was recovered in this pass. The calque is transparent — 锁定 ('lock on/lock in') is ordinary Chinese and 锁定效应 already exists in Chinese economics for path-dependent lock-in — so the words are available; what is missing is the discourse. The longtermist framing that motivates the term (very long time horizons, moral progress as a process that must be kept open) has little presence in Chinese AI-safety writing, which is oriented to nearer-term governance. terms.def: Alignment specifically to human ethical and social values, as distinct from alignment to a user's instructions or a developer's intent. In Chinese usage it is the ethics-facing half of alignment: teaching a system right from wrong, cooperative behaviour, and conformity to socially shared values.
terms.pit: The single character 观 is load-bearing and routinely lost. 价值对齐 ('value alignment') is the broader technical term and is what TC260's national framework uses — its official English is 'value alignment'; 价值观对齐 ('values alignment', with 价值观 = a person's or society's set of values, a worldview) narrows it to the ethical/social register. Translating both as 'value alignment' erases the distinction. The deeper trap for English readers is scope: English 'alignment' is an umbrella covering goal-directedness, corrigibility, deceptive alignment and control, whereas 价值观对齐 in PRC policy usage is almost entirely about *content and ethics* — a system that produces socially acceptable outputs. A PRC document promising 价值观对齐 is not thereby promising anything about scheming or shutdown resistance; those sit under 失控 and 可控性. Beware too the political reading: in regulatory documents 价值观 can point at 社会主义核心价值观, so the term can be doing content-governance work rather than technical-alignment work. Read the surrounding sentence.

Using 验证 where you mean adversarial inter-state inspection loses the whole point; using 核查 for a technical property sounds like an audit.
